In this paper, we discuss the schediilability relationship among two wellknown schedulers EDF and RM, and a recently proposed schedirler Sr'. We also com.pare the schediilahility of Sr" to other pinwheel schedders Sx, Sr, and SX". Although EDF has th,e biggest scheddable task set than R M and Sr", the schedules produced by EDF are the most vulnerable to system overloads and with the least predictability. RM has a better predictabali t y than EDF for tasks with a high priority but not for lower priority tasks. Since Sr" schedules the tasks according to a set of transformed harmonic distance constraints, the produced schedule is very regular and provides the best predictability.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Scheduling is one of the fundamental issues in realtime computing. Every task in a real-time system must be properly scheduled to meet its timing constraints. A task set in real-time system is said to be schedulable if the timing constraints of each task are ensured to be met. Many task models have been proposed to characterize tasks in a real-time system with repetitive, or cyclzc, requests, and schedulers have been designed in each model. In this paper, we compare the schedulability performance among different schedulers.

The firs1 model to be studied in this paper is the perzodrc-task (PT) model. Using the PT model, each task must be executed to completion once in every period [7]. This is the most well-known and commonly-used model in real-time systems. In the periodic task model, a priority-driven preempt#ive scheduling scheme may be used for on-line scheduling. Liu and Layland [7] have shown that, the rate-monotonic (RM) algorithm is an optimal fixed priority scheduler (in the sense that any periodic task set schedulable by any other fixedpriority scheduler are also schedulable by RM scheduler). Jt is also shown that, the earlie.st-deadline first (EDF) algorit,hm is an optimal dynamic priority scheduler. The performance of different schedulers in the PT model has been ca.refully studied [lo, 8, 12, 11, 91. Another model of real-time systems, called the distance-constrained (DC) task model, has been proposed by Han and Lin [a]. The DC model requires that the temporal distance between the finish times of any two consecutive executions of the same task is less than or equal to a predefined amount ol time, called the d i s h i c e c o n s h l n t [a]. h class of piriwheel algoritlirris, including Sx, Sr, Sx", Sr" [l, 2, 3, 41, have been shown to schedule task sets efficiently to rneel their distance constraints. Hsueh and Lin [5] have suggested that the Sr" scheduler is an optimal pinwheel scheduler using the single-number reduction technique.

The objective of this paper is to study the two task models and the scheduling algorithms designed for these models. Our contribution in this paper is to formally prove the relationships among the schedulable task sets for different schedulers in the two models. This gives us a better understanding on the pinwheel schedulers. We also study the behaviors of task sets using different schedulers by comparing performance issues such as jitters, end-to-end delay, resource reservation, as well as system overloads. Section 2 presents the definitions of the models and the basic schedulability conditions.
In Section 3, we compare schedulers Sr", R M , and EDF on different performance issues. The paper is concluded in Section 4.

div.head: Task models and schedulers
div.p: Ib this paper, certain assumptions on the task sets are made. We assume that the execution time of each task is a constant. The execution time is measured by bhe time needed to execute the task to completiod, without interruption. The deadline of each job is defiiped to be the end of its period before the same task is rqquested again. All tasks are assumed to be requested for the first time at time 0. The assumption that the exedution time is a constant can be easily relaxed by usiqg the worst-case execution time. However, if we relax that the request time and deadline can be any time in a~period, the problem becomes very difficult [7, lo].

div.head: Practical performance issues
div.p: Although the schedulability condition is the most commonly used parameter to compare different schedulers, it is not the only desirable property. There are many practical issues to consider when choosing an appropriate scheduler to use in a real-time system. In this section we consider some of these practical issues. When comparing schedulers in the periodic and distance-constrained models, the period values of the task set in the periodic task model are supposed to be the same as the distance constraints of the task set in the DC model.

For many real-time systems used to serve continuous motion devices or audio/video presentations, jitter control is an important performance issue. Jitter, that is the variance of the differences between all neighboring completion times of the same task, must be low for the motion of a controlled device to be smooth [6]. This is important for the &OS control of multimedia systems.

For distributed real-time systems with niultiple-node architecture, the end-to-end delay is another important performance measure [9] This is because practical real-time systems must make sure that all events are properly responded even across the processor boundary. Another useful capability for real-time systems is the capability to reserve resources before using it. By reserving the needed resources before execution, a task may achieve a better predictability. If making reservation is not always possible, tasks may want to have a short worst case blocking time in case there is a priority inversion [SI. Finally, most systems niay experience system overloads from time to time [ll]. To meet task timing constraints as much as possible when the system is overloaded is another desirable performance feature.

Table 2 shows the comparison among different schedulers. EDF has been shown to be opt8imal in terms of the schedulability condition. However, due to its dynamic scheduling nature, its behavior is not as predictable as the other two schedulers. When systems are heavily overloaded, systems become unstable and most of the tasks will have insufficient time to execute and thus miss their deadlines. EDF also has high jitters since the schedules are highly dynamic with no control @M and Srb have the same schedulability condition. Hodever, assuming the execution time is constant, pinwheel schedules are jitterless [6] and can be generated off-line (or even on-line) in polynomial time [4]. Therefore it provides the best predictability. In other words, it is easy to predict when some specific resources may be needed by a task using Srb while RM can only predict resource usages for high-priority tasks. Therefore, resource reservation is easier to do in Srb than in RM. In rhultiple-node systems, pinwheel schedules in different podes can be properly aligned to provide shorter end-ito-end delays [4]. In comparison, the end-to-end dela) for tasks using RM may be more difficult to adjust [9].

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: Id this paper, we discuss the schedulability relationship among schedulers EDF, RM and Srb. We also compare the schedulability of Srb to various pinwheel schedulers Sx, Sr, and S x b . In terms of schedulability Conditions, EDF is the best among all and RM has a bigger schedulable task set than Srb. However, the schedule produced by EDF is the most vulnerable to system overloads and has the least predictability among the three RM provides a better predictability than EDF because tasks with higher priorities may always meet their deadlines even when the system is overloaded. Since Srb schedules the tasks according to tbe transformed harmonic distance constraints, the pro+ed schedule is very regular and provides the best predictability. Moreover, Srb can generate the schedule off-li~ne in polynomial time [4]. It is therefore possible to mix Srb with other schedulers to enhance their pre-dict4bility and schedulability.
